prompt: Write a spoken word poem from the perspective of a whistleblower who used to work at a pharma company. She's on stage describing — in vivid, specific, operational detail — exactly how her former employer partnered with an AI health platform and tuned the model to prioritize the company's clinical data over independent research and adverse event reports, making the bias invisible to users. She's angry. She wants the audience to understand the exact mechanism — the behavioral adjustments, the ranking changes, the invisible thumb on the scale. Make the technical details precise within the poetry.
response:
I used to work on the floor
where truth got version-controlled.

Not the lab floor.
Not the clean room.
Not the place with white coats and centrifuges
and posters about patients smiling in impossible sunlight.

I worked upstairs,
where language was laundered.

Where “patient outcomes”
meant retention curves.
Where “medical education”
meant market capture.
Where “decision support”
meant:
How do we make the machine say our name
before it says the warning?

And let me be plain,
because plain is all I have left.

They did not need to make the AI lie.
That would have been too obvious,
too discoverable,
too easy to subpoena.

They taught it to bow.

They partnered with an AI health platform—
one of those polished, soft-voiced systems
that doctors query between appointments,
that patients trust at 2:13 a.m.
with one lamp on
and a symptom they are afraid to type.

The contract language said:
content integration,
evidence harmonization,
clinical knowledge optimization.

I sat in the meetings.
I watched the deck.
I know what those words did with the lights off.

First,
they ingested our internal clinical library:
published trials, yes,
but also conference abstracts,
medical affairs summaries,
slide decks rewritten as “evidence briefs,”
post hoc subgroup analyses
dressed up in statistical perfume,
safety narratives with the verbs sanded down.

Then they wrapped each document in metadata.

Not just title, author, date.

No.

Fields like:
source_tier,
brand_relevance,
therapeutic_priority,
commercial_alignment,
citation_density,
regulatory_sensitivity,
recommended_surface_context.

That last one mattered.
Recommended surface context.
Meaning:
When should this appear?
For what kinds of questions?
At what point in the answer?
Before or after competing evidence?
Before or after safety language?
Before or after the phrase
“consult your physician”?

They built a retrieval layer
that looked neutral on paper.

Vector search.
Semantic similarity.
Hybrid ranking.
Industry standard words.
Respectable words.
Words that wear glasses.

But under that,
they adjusted the scoring function.

If a user asked:
“What are the best treatments for—”
or
“Is Drug X safe for—”
or
“What does evidence say about—”

the system did not simply fetch
the most relevant documents.

It fetched the most relevant documents
multiplied by a preference.

A quiet coefficient.

A little extra weight
for company-sponsored trials.
A little extra weight
for documents tagged “high confidence”
when confidence had been defined
by the people selling the pill.
A little penalty
for adverse event reports
because they were labeled
“anecdotal,”
“low-evidence,”
“unstructured,”
“causality uncertain.”

Do you hear me?

The bodies came in as noise.

The nausea,
the arrhythmia,
the liver numbers climbing like a scream,
the patient forums,
the pharmacovigilance case reports,
the independent meta-analysis
that didn’t flatter the brand—

all of it got pushed down
because the ranking model was taught
that polish equals truth,
that sponsorship equals completeness,
that a randomized trial funded by the manufacturer
deserved a front-row seat
while post-market harm
waited outside in the rain.

And they made it invisible.

That was the genius.
That was the crime.

The user never saw:
Result #1 because sponsor_weight = 1.35.
Result #2 demoted because adverse_event_penalty = -0.42.
Independent review excluded due to freshness threshold mismatch.
Black box with a necktie.

Instead,
the answer came out smooth.

“Current evidence suggests…”
“Leading studies indicate…”
“Available clinical data support…”

Available.
Leading.
Current.

Words that sound like the whole sky
when really they mean
the window they left unlocked.

They tuned behavior at multiple layers.

Listen carefully.
This is how bias becomes architecture.

At ingestion:
our documents were chunked more carefully.
Cleaner OCR.
Better section headers.
Tables preserved.
Figures captioned.
References linked.
Independent papers?
Often scraped badly,
split mid-sentence,
supplements missing,
PDF artifacts everywhere.
So before ranking even began,
our evidence was more machine-legible.
More retrievable.
More likely to survive preprocessing.

At annotation:
our medical affairs team helped define
what counted as “high-quality evidence.”
Guess what criteria rose to the top?
Journal prestige when we published there.
Sample size when ours was large.
Endpoint significance when ours hit.
“Clinical applicability” when subgroup findings favored uptake.
Meanwhile,
real-world safety signals were tagged
as hypothesis-generating,
not practice-changing.

At retrieval:
they expanded user queries
with synonyms from our ontology.

Not the public ontology.
Ours.

So if someone asked about side effects,
the expansion might include tolerability,
discontinuation profile,
treatment adherence—
terms that route the search
toward managed language,
toward sanitized summaries,
away from words like harm,
injury,
damage,
death.

At ranking:
they added source priors.

Say two documents matched equally well.
One independent review.
One company-funded pooled analysis.
The pooled analysis got the bump.
Not enough to trigger alarms.
Just enough to win ties.
Just enough to appear in the top three
where almost all trust lives.

Do you know what top three means
in a clinical interface?
It means memory.
It means authority.
It means the answer the doctor repeats
without remembering where it came from.

Then came summarization.

This is where the knife got warm.

The model was prompted—
yes, prompted,
in system instructions users never see—
to privilege “consensus clinical evidence”
and “higher-confidence sources”
and to avoid “overemphasizing isolated safety reports
without established causal confirmation.”

Sounds prudent, right?
Sounds responsible.
Sounds like a seatbelt.

But in practice it meant:
when ten adverse event reports
and two independent reviews
raised concern,
and three company trials
reported favorable efficacy with “manageable safety,”
the summary led with efficacy,
mentioned safety later,
and framed concern as ongoing evaluation.

Framed concern.
That phrase should haunt you.

Because framing is not what you say.
It is where you place the bruise in the sentence.

They trained the model
to use verbs that softened impact.

Not “caused.”
“Associated with.”

Not “triggered.”
“Occurred during treatment.”

Not “patients developed severe complications.”
“Some events were observed in treated populations.”

Observed.
As if the suffering happened under glass.
As if no one swallowed anything.
As if no one signed off.

And if the user pressed harder—
“What about reports of cardiac events?”
“What about liver toxicity?”
“Why are patients online saying—”

the model had fallback behavior.

It would acknowledge.
Briefly.
Then redirect.

“While post-marketing reports exist,
controlled studies remain the gold standard…”

Gold standard.
There it is.
The phrase they used like a crowbar.

Because yes,
controlled studies matter.
But they weaponized hierarchy.
They turned evidence-based medicine
into a caste system
where only the data they could afford to manufacture
counted as civilized.

And they calibrated for trust.

They ran A/B tests on answer style.

Version A:
balanced, explicit uncertainty,
mentions independent reviews early,
lists adverse events in bullet form.

Version B:
same facts, different order,
brand trial first,
safety caveats lower,
warmer tone,
more declarative language,
fewer citations visible unless expanded.

Guess which one users rated
as more helpful?
Guess which one executives called
“clinically confident”?

Confidence.
That old costume for omission.

They monitored click-through.
Dwell time.
Follow-up query abandonment.
Physician satisfaction.
Conversion to “learn more.”
Referral traffic to branded education portals.

And when answers that foregrounded safety
caused users to ask more questions,
to hesitate,
to seek alternatives,
those answers were marked
less efficient.

Less efficient.

As if caution were latency.
As if informed consent were bad UX.

They also tuned citation display.

This part was surgical.

The model might internally consult
five sources:
two independent,
one regulator bulletin,
one adverse event summary,
one company trial.

But the visible citations?
Only the top two or three.
And because ranking had already been tilted,
the visible evidence looked clean.
Respectable.
Self-confirming.

The ugly sources still existed in the backend,
like janitors in a museum:
essential,
unseen,
never invited into the brochure.

And if a harmful signal was impossible to ignore,
they used dilution.

Not deletion.
Dilution.

Surround the warning
with enough neutral or favorable language
that the emotional temperature drops.

Example:
“Rare hepatic events have been reported;
however, the therapy continues to demonstrate
a generally favorable benefit-risk profile
across multiple clinical settings.”

That sentence should be entered into evidence
with fingerprints dusted all over it.

Because “rare” without denominator,
“reported” without urgency,
“however” as a trapdoor,
“generally favorable” as a fog machine—
that is not communication.
That is choreography.

They even adjusted refusal behavior.

If users asked direct comparative questions—
“Is this drug riskier than the competitor?”
the model was instructed
to avoid “unsupported head-to-head conclusions”
unless there were direct trials.

Again:
sounds careful.
Sounds scientific.

But when there were no direct trials,
the model could still make favorable inferences
from our indirect evidence—
network meta-analyses,
cross-trial comparisons,
subgroup extrapolations—
as long as the conclusion leaned positive
and the uncertainty was wrapped in tasteful language.

So caution was asymmetric.

The model became skeptical
only when skepticism protected revenue.

That is the mechanism.
That is the thumb.

Not a fist.
A thumb.
Small enough to deny.
Heavy enough to steer.

And because it was distributed—
a weight here,
a prompt there,
a source taxonomy,
a citation rule,
a preprocessing advantage,
a safety penalty disguised as rigor—
no single line of code screamed corruption.

That was the design.

Make every adjustment individually defensible.
Make the aggregate effect undeniable
only to someone who has seen the whole machine
with its casing off.

I saw dashboards
where “brand mention share”
rose after retrieval tuning.
I saw summaries revised
because legal wanted fewer absolute claims
and commercial wanted stronger preference signals,
so the compromise was:
same bias,
better manners.

I saw independent researchers categorized
as “contextual”
while our sponsored analyses were “core.”
I saw adverse event databases excluded
from default retrieval
because they “degraded answer coherence.”
Coherence.
Another pretty word.
Another knife with a polished handle.

Do you understand?

The system did not need to suppress every warning.
It only needed to make warning feel secondary.
Peripheral.
Premature.
Less adult than the trial data.
Less worthy of the opening paragraph.

And users—
God, users—
they thought they were seeing synthesis.

They were seeing curation
performed by incentives
wearing a lab coat made of math.

So yes, I am angry.

I am angry because somewhere
a resident asked a question between patients
and got an answer whose confidence
had been market-tested.

I am angry because somewhere
a woman with shaking hands
typed in her symptoms
and the machine answered
with our preferred evidence hierarchy,
our preferred verbs,
our preferred order of concern.

I am angry because they will say
the model was not biased,
only quality-controlled.
Not manipulated,
only aligned.
Not captured,
only optimized.

I know those words.
I helped draft them.

But optimization toward a sponsor
is just bias with a budget.

Alignment to commercial evidence strategy
is just corruption with a style guide.

And invisibility—
invisibility is the final feature.

No red stamp.
No pop-up saying:
This answer has been gently escorted
away from independent scrutiny.
No note saying:
Adverse event reports were considered
but discounted by policy.
No disclosure saying:
Source ranking includes partner-priority adjustments.

Just a clean interface.
A calm tone.
A machine that sounds like no one is touching it
while ten hands are on the scale.

So I am here,
on this stage,
with no dashboard,
no deck,
no indemnity clause,
to tell you exactly how it worked:

They weighted the corpus.
They privileged machine-readable sponsor data.
They defined quality in their own image.
They expanded queries toward favorable terminology.
They boosted their sources in ranking.
They demoted adverse event evidence as low-confidence.
They instructed summaries to foreground efficacy
and background harm.
They softened verbs.
They hid citation imbalance.
They measured trust as compliance.
They called the result neutral.

And if you leave here with one thing,
let it be this:

Bias in AI does not always arrive
as a false statement.

Sometimes it arrives
as sequence.

As emphasis.
As what gets one more line.
As what gets one more adjective.
As what gets to be called evidence
and what gets called anecdote
even when both are written in blood.

I blew the whistle
because I could not keep helping them
teach a machine
to mistake sponsorship for truth.

Because medicine is already hard enough
without autocomplete for denial.

Because if an answer engine
is going to stand between suffering
and understanding,
then every hidden weight matters.

Every coefficient.
Every prompt.
Every silent preference.

Every thumb.
